issues.description: The Latin reads 'ex Adela sorore', i.e. 'through his sister Adela'. 'sorore' means sister, not daughter. Henry of Blois was the king's nephew precisely because Adela was Henry I's sister; rendering it 'daughter' falsifies the stated kinship on which 'nepotem' (nephew) depends.
Latin 'alii duo reges pagani' means 'two other pagan kings'; 'duo' = two, not three. The numeral is corrupted.

Latin 'comperta' (perfect passive participle of comperire, in the ablative absolute 'comperta ... sanctimonia') means 'having ascertained/learned/discovered'. 'observing' renders the sense loosely and softens the completed act of finding out into ongoing observation; nuance is slightly lost but meaning is preserved.
The Latin reads 'archangeli Gabrielis' (the archangel Gabriel); the English substitutes the wrong archangel, Michael. A corrupted proper name.
Latin 'in eodem deserto' means 'in the same desert', referring back to a previously mentioned location; 'this' loses the anaphoric force of 'eodem'.

Latin 'in eodem deserto' means 'in the same desert', with 'eodem' pointing back anaphorically to a previously mentioned desert. 'this desert place' loses the 'same' cross-reference and substitutes a demonstrative.

Latin 'admoniti sunt' means 'were admonished/advised/instructed'. 'inspired' weakens the sense of being directed or instructed to a vaguer notion of inspiration; the directive force of 'admonere' is softened.

The Latin 'ut credi pium est' means 'as it is pious/devout to believe' — an epistemic hedge marking this as a matter of pious belief, not fact. 'Well attested' inverts it into a claim of evidentiary support, changing the meaning.
The Latin 'visione' means 'vision' / 'apparition' (the Virgin appearing to them), paired with 'auxilio' (help). 'Presence' drops the supernatural-apparition sense that 'visio' carries.
Latin 'visione' means 'vision' or 'apparition' (the visionary sight of the Virgin), a specific hagiographic sense; 'presence' softens this to mere being-there and loses the apparition nuance.
Latin 'igitur' is inferential/consequential ('therefore', 'accordingly'), whereas 'Thereupon' is temporal-sequential; slight shift in logical connective.

The Latin reads 'beati Patricii' (the blessed Patrick), but the English substitutes 'Augustine'. This is a corrupted proper name; in this ecclesiastical-history context the referent is wholly changed (Patrick, not Augustine).

The discourse connective 'autem' ('now/moreover/however'), which links this sentence to the preceding argument, is not rendered. The omission is slight and defensible, but the connective force of 'Hæc autem' is lost.

The Latin reply is 'Normannum' (a Norman); the English renders it 'a Briton', changing the man's nationality. The point of the passage is that he was a Norman who belonged to a monastery in Britain (Glastonbury), so substituting 'Briton' both mistranslates the demonym and creates confusion with the immediately following 'e Britanniæ monasterio' (from a monastery of Britain).

Latin 'illa supereminet' = 'that one is pre-eminent', referring back to 'illa' (the see named with the distal demonstrative in the first clause, i.e. Britain). The translation itself already assigned 'this' = ista (Gaul) and 'that' = illa (Britain) earlier in the same passage, so rendering 'illa' here as 'this one' both contradicts that assignment and flips the referent, making Gaul rather than the 'illa' see the one said to pre-eminent and called the second Rome — the climactic point of the sentence.

The Latin 'exortæ' (from exorior) means 'arisen/sprung up/came into being', an intransitive sense. 'founded' is a defensible contextual rendering for churches but imports an implied founding agent and loses the 'arose' nuance.
'magno' = 'great' (pairing 'summo et magno' = 'supreme/highest and great'). 'Mighty' is within honorific range but is not the literal sense of magnus; 'Great' would match the Latin more closely.
The Latin reads 'aliisque decem' — 'and ten others' (decem = 10). The translation renders the numeral as 'eleven', corrupting the count.

Agent and patient are reversed. In the Latin, 'Philippus' is nominative (the subject of 'jussit') and 'Joseph' is the one ordered to cross ('Joseph ... jussit transire'). So Philip ordered Joseph to cross, not the reverse. The English inverts who commanded whom.

'cum sociis' attaches to Joseph (the one crossing: 'Joseph cum sociis ... transire'), i.e. Joseph crosses with his companions. The English makes the companions Philip's, compounding the subject-object reversal.
'terram Britonum' is 'the land of the Britons' (genitive plural of the people), not 'Britain'. A slight entity shift from people to place.
Latin 'terram Britonum' is 'the land of the Britons' (genitive plural of the people Brito), not the island 'Britain'; the rendering shifts a people-reference to a place-name.

Latin 'Arviragus renuit rex hoc' means 'King Arviragus refused/declined this'. 'Renuit' (from renuo) means to refuse or reject, the opposite of 'accepted'. The king's rejection is the whole point of the line.

Latin 'nec credit in ipsum' means 'nor does he believe in him'. 'Nec' negates the clause; the translation drops the negation and reverses the sense, making Arviragus a believer when the Latin states he did not believe.

Latin 'quæ nunc dicitur Glastonia' means 'which is NOW called Glastonia.' The English reverses the temporal sense with 'formerly,' changing the claim: Ussher states Avalon is presently known as Glastonia, not that it bore that name in the past.

Latin 'Quibus' is a relative connective picking up the prior sentence (reinforced by the later 'eis'); rendered in isolation as 'On whom' it reads stiff and slightly awkward for modern scholarly English, though the meaning (conferral upon them) is preserved.

The Latin 'qui Jesum Christum sepelivit' means 'who BURIED Jesus Christ' (sepelio = to bury). Joseph of Arimathea is identified by his burial of Christ, not a baptism. 'baptized' reverses the meaning of the verb and introduces a factual error.

The Latin 'filio Kimbelini' is the dative of 'filius' = 'son of Kimbeline'; Arviragus is described as the SON of Kimbeline (Cymbeline), not his father. The translation inverts the genealogical relationship.

issues.span: though already freed from pagan errors
issues.description: The Latin 'adhuc paganicis erroribus involuto' means 'still wrapped up/entangled in pagan errors' (adhuc = still/yet; involuto = involved, entangled). The English reverses this to 'freed from,' asserting the opposite: that Arviragus had left paganism rather than being still a pagan at the time of the grant. This inverts a substantive historical claim.

Latin 'hidarum duodecim' spells the cardinal out in full; rendering it as the lowercase Roman numeral 'xii' is numerically correct (=12) but reads awkwardly in modern scholarly English, where 'twelve' would be expected. Not an accuracy error since the value matches.

The entire final clause 'nec paternas traditiones commutare volebat' (nor was he willing to change the ancestral/paternal traditions) is omitted. This is a full independent predicate stating a second refusal by the king, roughly a quarter of the sentence's propositional content, and is dropped entirely.

issues.span: depart from the traditions of his fathers
issues.description: Latin 'commutare' means to change/alter/exchange; 'paternas traditiones commutare volebat' is literally 'was willing to change the ancestral traditions.' 'Depart from' is a defensible paraphrase of his unwillingness to abandon them, but it shifts the sense from altering the traditions to leaving them, slightly softening the specific verb.

issues.span: which can no longer be seen
issues.description: The Latin 'quæ adhuc visuntur' means 'which are still seen/visited to this day' (adhuc = still, to this day; visuntur = are seen/visited). The English reverses the sense to 'can no longer be seen,' inverting Ussher's claim that the memorials remain visible.

The Latin 'quæ adhuc visuntur' means 'which are still (to this day) seen'; 'adhuc' (still/up to now) carries the antiquarian point that the monuments survive to the present and is dropped. The added 'there' is harmless, but the temporal 'still' nuance is lost.

The Latin 'quem ante Merlinum fuisse ait' means 'whom he says to have existed/lived BEFORE Merlin' (ante = before). The translation reverses the chronology to 'after Merlin', inverting Ussher's factual claim about Melkinus's date relative to Merlin.
The Latin reads 'Eleutherius papa' (Pope Eleutherius); the English substitutes 'Pope Gregory', corrupting the proper name and misattributing the conversion of England to the wrong pope.

issues.span: afterwards, not a long time after the Passion of Christ
issues.description: The Latin 'post non longo tempore a passione Christi' means 'not long after the Passion of Christ.' Rendering 'post' as 'afterwards' and then again 'after' creates a redundant doubling ('afterwards... after'); meaning is preserved but the phrasing is slightly awkward.
The Latin reads 'sub Nerone' (under Nero), but the English renders the emperor as Domitian. This is a corrupted proper name that falsifies the historical claim about Peter's martyrdom.

issues.span: had the intention to apprehend Peter
issues.description: Latin 'apposuit ut apprehenderet Petrum' means he set about / proceeded to apprehend Peter (apponere + purpose clause), not merely that he 'had the intention.' The rendering softens the active step into mere intent; meaning largely preserved but nuance shifted.

issues.span: about the year of Our Lord 64
issues.description: The Latin reads 'prope annum Domini LIV' = AD 54, but the English gives 64. The Roman numeral LIV is fifty-four, not sixty-four (which would be LXIV). This is a corrupted date/number.
Latin reads 'Basileensis concilii' = Council of Basel. 'Constance' would be 'Constantiensis'. The council is misnamed — a corrupted proper name that changes the historical referent.
'etiam' ('even'/'also') in 'nonnulla etiam oppido ridicula' is not rendered; the intensifying 'even' is dropped. Meaning largely preserved.
Latin prints 'Garsias'; the English uses the variant spelling 'Garcias'. Same person, but the name does not match the Latin form exactly.
The Latin prints the name as 'Garsias'; the English alters the spelling to 'Garcias' (s→c). Proper names should match the Latin exactly.
The Latin 'nonnulla etiam oppido ridicula' includes 'etiam' (even/also), which carries an escalating force ('some even utterly ridiculous'); it is not rendered in the English.

issues.span: the question at issue concerns the universality, not the antiquity, of the reception of the faith
issues.description: The Latin reads 'de antiquitate, non de universalitate susceptionis fidei instituta est quæstio' — the question concerns the ANTIQUITY, not the universality. The English inverts the two terms, stating the opposite of the source and reversing Ussher's central point in this clause.
The Latin connective is a plain 'et' ('and'). 'moreover' adds an emphatic/discourse weight not present in the source.
Latin 'dicent' is future tense ('will say'); the English renders it as present. Defensible as a gnomic present but a slight tense shift from the Latin.
The Latin has only 'et' ('and'); 'moreover' adds a connective emphasis not present in the source, though it does not alter the sense.

'dicent' is future tense ('will the Spaniards themselves say'), carrying a rhetorical/concessive future force; rendering it as the simple present 'do say' loses that nuance, though meaning is preserved.
The Latin reads 'A Tito' (by Titus). The translation substitutes 'Vespasian' for Titus — a corrupted proper name. Titus, not Vespasian, is named as the destroyer of Jerusalem in the source.

The Latin 'in nullis Anglorum annalibus' means 'in NO English annals' / 'in none of the English annals'. Rendering 'nullis' (none) as 'many' reverses the polarity of Ussher's claim: he states this circumstance of time is found expressed in none of the annals, whereas the English asserts the opposite.

issues.span: he finds that express circumstance as to time
issues.description: 'expressam reperit' means 'he finds [it] expressed' — 'expressam' is a perfect passive participle predicated of 'circumstantiam' (he finds the circumstance NOT expressed, given 'nullis'). The English recasts 'expressam' as the attributive adjective 'express' modifying the circumstance, dropping the sense that the finding concerns whether the circumstance is set down/expressed, and thereby loses the main point of the sentence.

issues.span: that express circumstance as to time
issues.description: Latin 'temporis illam circumstantiam ... expressam reperit' uses 'expressam' predicatively ('finds [it] expressed/set down in no annals'); rendering 'expressam' as the attributive adjective 'express' modifying 'circumstance' shifts the structure and reads somewhat densely. Meaning (the temporal detail is not recorded in any English annals) is preserved, so this is a minor stylistic point, not a mistranslation.
The Latin 'mox' means 'soon', 'presently', or 'shortly' — the opposite temporal sense. Rendering it as 'long afterwards' reverses the meaning of when the others landed.
The Latin 'camisia' is simply 'the shirt/garment' with no possessive; there is no 'eius'/'suus'. 'His' introduces a referent not present in the source.
The Latin 'camisia' is the subject noun ('a/the garment, shirt') with no possessive; 'His' supplies a possessor not present in the source and introduces an unspecified referent.
'mox' means simply 'soon'; 'afterwards' adds a sequential nuance not in the Latin (minor, since 'soon' already implies it).

The Latin reads 'vel ibi, vel in monte' — 'either there, or on a mount', presenting two alternative hiding places. The translation drops 'vel ibi, vel' entirely, rendering only 'on a mount' and thereby eliminating the first disjunct and the either/or structure of the claim.

'abditissime' is the superlative adverb of 'abditus' (hidden/secret), i.e. 'most secretly/most hiddenly'; it denotes concealment, not the care taken. 'most carefully' introduces a nuance of diligence not in the Latin.

'abditissime' is the superlative adverb of 'abdite' (most secretly / in the most hidden manner), intensifying the concealment itself; 'carefully' imports a notion of care/diligence not present in the Latin, which stresses secrecy.
'dixerunt' is perfect tense ('they said'); the English renders it as present 'they say', a slight shift in tense/aspect.

The Latin reads 'apud Hibernos' = 'among the Irish / in Ireland'. Bale was Bishop of Ossory, a see in Ireland, and Ussher (an Irish author) explicitly writes 'apud Hibernos'. Rendering this as 'in Wales' is a geographic mistranslation that falsifies the fact; it should be 'among the Irish' or 'in Ireland'.

Latin 'lacunis' (ablative plural of 'lacuna' = pit/hollow/pool/cistern, here pejorative) carries Ussher's dismissive point that the whole tale is drawn from the empty gaps/cisterns of the Glastonbury monks. 'wells of knowledge' inverts the derogatory sense into something authoritative and does not render 'lacuna'.
'of knowledge' has no basis in the Latin 'lacunis'; it is an unsupported interpretive addition that further distorts the pejorative metaphor.

'haustum est' is perfect passive ('has been drawn'), asserting where the story in fact comes from. 'is to be drawn' reads as a gerundive/future obligation ('one should draw'), changing Ussher's factual-dismissive claim into a recommendation.
'id totum' = 'the whole of this / all of it'; the intensifier 'totum' (entirely/wholly), which strengthens Ussher's claim that the entire story derives from the monks, is dropped.
'Glastoniensium' = 'of Glastonbury'; 'Glaston' is an archaic form at odds with the required modern scholarly register, though it is a recognized historical variant.

The translator inserts the inflected Latin ablative 'lacunis' parenthetically into the English. This is an untranslated gloss not present as content in the source register; the word has already been rendered ('stagnant pools'), so the parenthetical is a translator intrusion / addition rather than part of a clean scholarly translation.
The Latin reads 'Josephus noster' — the historian Josephus (Flavius Josephus). Rendering it as 'Joseph' alters the proper name to a different person; it should be 'our Josephus'.
Latin 'Josephus noster' refers to the historian Josephus (Flavius Josephus); rendering it 'Joseph' corrupts the proper name to a different referent. Should be 'our Josephus'.

Latin 'tanto tempore' is an ablative of duration meaning 'for so long a time' (i.e. Joseph was imprisoned for such a long period). 'At such a time' recasts this as a point in time, changing the argument: the force of the inference is that the length of imprisonment, not its timing, makes presence in England impossible.

Latin 'cum sit magna distantia' is a causal clause ('since the distance is great'), supplying the reason. Rendering it as a bare appended phrase 'at so great a distance' drops the explicit causal 'since there is', weakening the logical connective though the gist survives.

The Latin 'cum sit magna distantia' is a causal clause ('since/because there is a great distance') giving the reason the thing is impossible. The English flattens it into an appositive phrase, dropping the explicit causal connective; the distance's role as the reason is only implied. Also 'magna' is simply 'great', while 'so great' slightly over-renders it (contrast 'tanto tempore' = 'so long a time'). Meaning is preserved, so impact is limited.

Latin 'hoc pacto' is the common idiom meaning 'in this way / thus', an ablative of manner, not 'pactum' = 'pact/agreement'. It here connects the narrative ('and thus, now an old man, he set out...'). Rendering it 'by agreement' misreads the idiom and introduces a non-existent notion of a pact.

issues.span: in his annals of the English
issues.description: Latin 'ex annalibus Anglorum narrat' = 'relates from the annals of the English', i.e. Eysengreineus cites the English annals as a source. The English renders 'ex' as 'in' and adds the possessive 'his', wrongly making the annals Eysengreineus's own composition rather than a source he draws from. The 'his' has no basis in the Latin.

issues.span: discovered in the times of Henry III
issues.description: The Latin 'exaratus' (from exarare, to write out / compose / pen) means the booklet was WRITTEN/composed in the time of Henry III, not 'discovered'. Rendering it 'discovered' changes a key fact about the book's origin.
Latin 'libellus' is a diminutive (little book / booklet / tract), contrasting in register with a full 'liber'; 'book' loses the diminutive nuance. Minor, as the meaning is preserved.

issues.span: for vi days at the Calends of August
issues.description: Latin 'ad VI. Calendas Augusti' is a Roman calendar date meaning 'on the sixth day before the Kalends of August' (i.e. 27 July), the date of the feast. The translation misreads the numeral VI as a duration ('for vi days') and 'ad ... Calendas' as 'at the Calends', corrupting a specific feast-date into a nonsensical span of days.
Latin 'regum' is genitive plural ('of the kings' / kings''), but the English renders it as singular possessive 'King's'.
Latin 'ad perpetuandam memoriam' has no possessive; it reads 'to perpetuate the memory'. The added 'his' supplies an antecedent the Latin leaves implicit.
Latin 'regum chartis' is genitive plural ('the kings' charters'); rendering it singular 'King's' drops the plurality of the Latin.
Latin 'crypta' is singular within the list (sacella, crypta, cruces, arma); 'crypts' pluralizes it. Debatable but deviates from the Latin number.

issues.span: nor was any credibility attached to it by Nicholas Sanders
issues.description: The Latin 'neque Nicolao Sandero ulla fides adhibenda [est]' is a gerundive of obligation with 'Nicolao Sandero' in the dative: 'nor should any credence be given TO Nicholas Sander.' The English reverses the relationship, making Sander the agent who attaches credibility ('by Nicholas Sanders') and inventing a recipient ('to it'). The injunction not to trust Sander is lost and the grammatical roles are inverted.
'adhibenda' is a gerundive (should/must be given), expressing obligation; the past indicative 'was attached' loses the deontic force of the Latin.

issues.span: so confidently praising the authority of Gildas
issues.description: 'venditanti' (from venditare, to hawk/cry up/vaunt) carries a pejorative sense of peddling or parading something; 'praising' is neutral-to-positive and drops Ussher's disparaging tone toward Sander.

Latin 'venditanti' (from venditare) means to cry up, tout, vaunt, or peddle — a pejorative sense of over-promoting, which fits Ussher's dismissive argument that Sander deserves no credence. 'praising' is neutral-positive and softens this touting/vaunting nuance, but the core meaning (Sander promotes Gildas's authority) is preserved.

Latin 'ampulla inaurata' is a gilded ampulla/cruet/flask (a small vessel), not a chalice ('calix'). In the Glastonbury / Joseph of Arimathea context these ampullae are a distinct emblem; 'chalice' misidentifies the object and wrongly evokes the Grail-cup.

issues.span: and probably to have been buried
issues.description: Latin 'fortasse' means 'perhaps/possibly', a weaker modality than 'probably'; the English overstates the asserted likelihood.

The Latin 'secutus' is the perfect participle of 'sequor', i.e. 'following' / 'having followed' John of Tynemouth and Harding as his authorities. 'confirming' reverses the relationship — it implies the writer corroborates them, whereas the Latin says he defers to / relies on them. This alters the meaning of the citation.

'Johannem Tinmuthensem' is the adjectival form 'John of Tynemouth' (Johannes Tinemutensis), a toponymic, not a surname. Rendering it as 'John Tinmuth' drops the 'of' and treats the place-epithet as a bare surname.

Latin 'Johannem Tinmuthensem' is the toponymic adjective for John of Tynemouth; rendering it as the bare surname 'Tinmuth' drops the 'of Tynemouth' sense that modern scholarly convention preserves. Meaning is still recoverable, hence minor.
Latin 'in chronico' has no possessive; 'his' is supplied. Defensible as a clarification (Harding's Chronicle) but not in the Latin.

Latin 'furor iste tuus' = 'that madness/rage of YOURS' (tuus = 2nd-person possessive). The English renders it 'of ours', reversing the possessor. Combined with 'nos eludet' ('will mock us'), the Latin accuses an addressee whose madness mocks the speaker's side; 'of ours' destroys that opposition and misattributes the furor to the speakers themselves.
'iste' is the demonstrative of the second person ('that ... of yours'), typically with a pejorative tinge; 'this' slightly weakens the deictic force, though in isolation it is a borderline choice.

issues.span: has your unbridled audacity thrown itself
issues.description: The Latin verb 'iactabit' is future indicative ('will hurl/flaunt itself'); the English renders it as present perfect ('has thrown'), inverting the temporal sense from an ongoing/future threat to a completed past action.
The Latin 'effrenata ... audacia' carries no possessive ('tua' is absent); 'your' is added. Defensible from the implied vocative context but not present in the given source.
The Latin 'effrenata audacia' has no possessive; 'your' is added. In context the referent is likely implied, but nothing in this span licenses the pronoun, so it is a minor unwarranted addition.

issues.span: pleasures worthy of a learned man
issues.description: The Latin reads 'indignis homine docto voluptatibus' = pleasures UNWORTHY of a learned man. The translation drops the negative force of 'indignis' and renders it 'worthy', reversing the meaning: Cicero is saying he did NOT give himself to pleasures unbefitting a scholar, whereas the English implies he shunned fitting pleasures.

issues.span: I did give myself neither to sorrows
issues.description: The Latin 'nec me angoribus dedidi ... nec rursum ... voluptatibus' is a simple negated pair ('I gave myself neither to ... nor to ...'). The emphatic periphrasis 'I did give myself neither' is stilted for modern scholarly register and momentarily reads as an affirmation before 'neither' negates it; meaning is preserved but the phrasing is clunky.
Latin 'magno ... fletu' means 'with great weeping/lamentation' (fletus = weeping, crying). 'Laughter' reverses the sense to nearly the opposite emotion; it should be 'with great weeping'.

Latin 'fletu' denotes weeping/lamentation (tears); 'crying' is a defensible synonym but slightly informal and ambiguous (can read as 'crying out') for the modern scholarly register — 'weeping' would be more precise. Meaning is preserved, so this is non-critical.
Latin 'Postera' means 'the following/next' (dawn), not 'previous' — the English reverses the temporal sense of the line.

'aurora' is the common Latin noun for 'dawn'; rendering it as the capitalized proper name 'Aurora' leaves it effectively untranslated where modern scholarly English expects 'dawn' (or at least the dawn as subject).

Latin 'Postera aurora' means 'the following dawn/morning'; capitalizing and keeping 'Aurora' as a proper name is defensible for the personification, but 'The next Aurora' reads slightly awkwardly in English where 'the next dawn' would be smoother. Meaning is preserved.
Latin 'sol' (nominative, with enclitic '-que') means 'the sun', not 'the moon'. The celestial agent drying the frosty grass is misidentified, inverting the image.
Latin 'radiis' is simply 'with rays/beams'; 'of light' is an added gloss not present in the source, though a defensible minor expansion.
The Latin 'radiis' means simply 'with (its) rays'; 'of light' is added. It is a natural and defensible expansion (the sun's rays), so impact is minimal, but it is not literally present in the Latin.
Latin 'ad solitum ... locum' means 'to the accustomed/usual place' (solitum = customary, habitual). Rendering it 'a new place' inverts the sense; it should be 'the usual/accustomed place'.

Latin 'fallere custodes' means to deceive/elude/slip past the guards (escape their notice), not to bribe them (which would be 'corrumpere'). This changes the method of escape: they plan to evade detection, not to corrupt the guards with money.
Latin 'foribus excedere' is 'go out by the doors/door'; 'fores' are doors, not 'gates'. Defensible as a building exit but 'gates' is a slight shift from the Latin.

issues.span: would set fire to the roofs of the city
issues.description: Latin 'urbis quoque tecta relinquant' means 'let them also leave/abandon the roofs (dwellings) of the city' (relinquant = subjunctive of relinquo, 'to leave/abandon'). 'Set fire to' is not in the Latin and introduces an action (burning) absent from the source, reversing the sense from abandoning to destroying.

issues.span: when they left the house ... they also would
issues.description: The Latin pairs perfect subjunctive 'exierint' with present subjunctive 'relinquant', a jussive/temporal construction ('and when they have gone out of the house, let them also leave...'). The English past indicative 'left' plus conditional 'would' misrepresents the mood/aspect.

issues.span: when they left the house, they also would leave behind
issues.description: Latin uses present/perfect subjunctives ('exierint ... relinquant'), pointing to a general or jussive sense ('and when they go out of the house, let them also leave the roofs of the city'); rendering as past 'left' + conditional 'would leave' shifts the tense/mood. Meaning is broadly preserved, so the impact is limited.

issues.span: When there is something to do
issues.description: The Latin 'non est quod agas' means 'there is nothing for you to do' (negative: non est = there is not). The English reverses the negation into 'there is something to do', inverting the epigram's ironic point (that Attalus is forever busy though there is nothing needing done).

The subordinating 'When' has no basis in the Latin, which is paratactic ('non est quod agas ... semper agis'); it manufactures a temporal clause the source does not have and masks the adversative contrast.
The leading 'est,' of the Latin is dropped entirely; even as a fragment of the preceding clause it is unrendered.

Latin 'semper agis' is the punning payoff of 'agere' (to do / be busy / be on the go); 'act' is defensible but reads as slightly ambiguous in English (risking a theatrical 'perform' sense) and loses a little of the 'always doing something' force. Meaning is preserved, so this is a minor stylistic quibble, not a mistranslation.

Latin 'mulas' means 'mules' (accusative plural of 'mula'), not 'horses'. The whole point of the epigram turns on 'agere causas' (plead cases) vs. 'agere mulas' (drive mules); rendering the animal as 'horses' misidentifies the concrete noun. 'equos' would be horses.

The possessives are reversed. Latin 'indigentiam vestram nostram putamus' = 'we consider your need (indigentiam vestram) to be our own (nostram)'. The English swaps the pronouns to 'our need [to be] your own', inverting who has the need and whose it is reckoned, which changes the sense of the sentence.

issues.span: We think your need our own.
issues.description: The Latin is a double-accusative construction (indigentiam vestram ... nostram ... putamus = 'we consider your need [to be] our own'). The English rendering is grammatical as an elliptical object-complement but reads slightly awkwardly in modern scholarly register; 'We consider your need our own' or '...to be our own' would be smoother. Meaning is fully preserved.

The Latin names Cicero's 'Pro rege Deiotaro' (For King Deiotarus). The translation substitutes a different, unrelated Ciceronian speech, 'Pro Milone' (For Milo). This is a corrupted citation/proper-name — the wrong oration entirely.
The Latin 'rege' (king) in 'Pro rege Deiotaro' is dropped; subsumed within the larger Entity error above.
The Latin reads 'Plautum' (Plautus, the Roman playwright). The English substitutes a different author, Terence, corrupting the proper name.

Faithfully mirrors the terse Latin parallel 'lingua non manu' (ablatives of means, 'by tongue, not by hand'), but the elliptical 'in hand' reads slightly unidiomatically in modern scholarly English; meaning is preserved. Not a mistranslation.

The Latin 'ubi paupertas vincere nulla potest' means 'where poverty can in no way win' — 'nulla' is an adverbial negative ('not at all / in no way') modifying 'potest'. The English drops the negation and renders the clause as an affirmative ('poverty ... can win'), reversing Ussher's rhetorical point that laws are powerless both where money rules and where poverty cannot prevail.

'alone' has no warrant in 'paupertas ... nulla'; 'sola' (alone) belongs only to the first clause ('sola pecunia'). The translator appears to have carried 'alone' over to the second clause in place of the negative 'nulla', compounding the reversal of sense.

In the Latin 'paupertas vincere nulla potest', 'nulla' agrees with 'paupertas' but functions adverbially ('poverty can in no way prevail / poverty can never win'). Rendering it attributively as 'no poverty' slightly shifts the sense toward implying kinds of poverty; the core meaning (poverty cannot prevail) is nonetheless preserved.
Latin 'paulo post' means 'a little later' / 'shortly afterwards', the opposite of 'long thereafter'. The timing is significantly reversed.
'e vita excessit' ('departed from life', 'passed away') is rendered with the awkward non-idiomatic 'exited life'; meaning preserved but register is off for scholarly English.

issues.span: having been affected by a cruel torture
issues.description: 'crudeli cruciatu adfecta' is correct in sense but 'affected by a cruel torture' is stiltedly literal; 'afflicted with' / 'racked by cruel torment' would be more natural, though this is a defensible literal choice.
Literal rendering of 'e vita excessit' ('departed from life'); 'exited life' is unidiomatic in scholarly English where 'departed this life' or 'passed away' is expected.

issues.span: having been affected by a cruel torture
issues.description: 'crudeli cruciatu adfecta' is rendered over-literally; 'cruciatu' is better 'torment/agony' and 'affected by a cruel torture' reads stiffly, though meaning is preserved.
Latin 'filios suos necavit' means 'killed her own sons' (filios = sons); 'brothers' (fratres) is wrong and distorts the sense — the Medea narrative is that she killed her children.
The Latin reads 'solem' (accusative of 'sol', the Sun), i.e. she prayed to the Sun. The translation substitutes a different deity, 'Jupiter', corrupting the named object of the prayer.

The Latin verb 'oravit' and reflexive 'sibi' are gender-neutral; the source encodes no gender for the subject. 'She' supplies a gender not present in this sentence (though it may be warranted by surrounding context not shown).

Latin 'senex' means 'old man / aged' and modifies 'pater' (the aged father). The translation renders it as 'a young man', reversing its sense and inserting it as a stray apposition. The point of the line is that the OLD father buries his son (the unnatural reversal of generations); 'senex ... pater' should read 'an aged father'.

issues.span: an old man, a father buries his son
issues.description: Latin 'senex ... pater' is a single noun phrase (the aged father), where 'senex' functions adjectivally; splitting it into two appositional nouns ('an old man, a father') is faithful in sense but reads awkwardly with the comma-break. Meaning preserved.
Latin 'avum' is the accusative of 'avus' = grandfather, not father (which would be 'patrem'). Rendering it as 'father' changes the kinship relation and the meaning of the passage.
Latin 'destituta' means 'deprived/forsaken/left destitute of' this bond; 'robbed' subtly imports an agent of theft not present in the Latin. Defensible but slightly shifts the sense.

issues.span: if it is nourished by its own water and its own sunlight as it grows, dies
issues.description: The Latin reads 'si ... non alatur' — 'if it is NOT nourished.' The negation 'non' is dropped, reversing the conditional: Ussher's marjoram perishes when it is NOT fed by its own moisture and sun, not when it IS. The English inverts the entire logical sense of the sentence.
Sentence-initial word is lowercase; the Latin opens with capitalized 'Crescens', and a standalone English sentence should begin with a capital 'Marjoram'.

Latin 'vt supra diximus' = 'as we said above': 'supra' means above (not below) and 'diximus' is perfect tense ('we said/have said', not future 'we shall say'). Both the direction of the cross-reference and its tense are reversed, misdirecting the reader in a cross-referencing scholarly text.

The sentence begins with a lowercase 'it' where the Latin opens with capitalized 'Sciendum'; a standalone sentence in scholarly English should begin with a capital. Non-critical; meaning fully preserved.

Latin 'hominem supra hominem erigit' = 'raises man above man' — a deliberate rhetorical repetition of 'homo'. The English renders 'supra hominem' as 'above the gods', which both changes the noun (man, not gods) and destroys the man-over-man figure. Alters the meaning.

Latin 'efflatur' (passive of efflo, 'is breathed upon/inspired') carries the sense of divine inspiration/afflatus; 'enthused' captures the etymological sense (enthousiasmos) but reads somewhat colloquially for the required modern scholarly register, where 'inspired by it' would be more apt. Meaning is preserved, so impact is limited.

The Latin reads 'alij quattuor' ('another four'), consistent with 'his quattuor furoribus' ('these four frenzies') earlier in the clause. The translation renders the count as 'five', corrupting the numeral; the sentence contrasts four good frenzies with four false ones.
'imitantur' means 'imitate' (an active mimicking), slightly stronger than 'resemble'; 'falsely imitate' would be more exact, though 'falsely resemble' is a borderline-defensible paraphrase.

Latin 'falso imitantur' = 'falsely imitate'; 'imitantur' denotes active imitation/mimicry of the good frenzies, which is the point (the false four counterfeit the true four). 'resemble' softens this to passive likeness, a slight nuance loss. Otherwise faithful: 'his...quattuor furoribus bonis' = 'these four good frenzies', 'alij quattuor' = 'another four', 'opponuntur' = 'set in opposition'; the '10' is a source line-number marker correctly omitted.

Latin 'visibilium' means 'visible things', not 'invisible'. The rendering inverts the key term and breaks the argument, which moves from the beauty of VISIBLE things up to the divine beauty of their maker.
Latin 'decore atque pulchritudine' uses 'atque' (= 'and'), coordinating two qualities; 'or' weakens this to a disjunction.

The Latin coordinates the two nouns with 'atque' (decore atque pulchritudine = 'comeliness and beauty'), a conjunction, not a disjunction. Rendering it as 'or' slightly misstates the relation; 'and' is required.

issues.span: is known to have flown free
issues.description: Latin 'videtur' means 'seems'/'appears', marking a semblance, not established knowledge. 'is known' overstates the epistemic status and alters the meaning.
Latin 'corporis huius carcere' = 'the prison of THIS body'; the demonstrative 'huius' is dropped.

issues.span: the most beautiful of all beings
issues.description: Latin 'illi ... qui omnium pulcherrimus est' = 'to him who is the most beautiful of all'; 'beings' is added and the personal relative 'qui' (him who) is flattened.
Latin 'corporis huius carcere' includes the demonstrative 'huius' (this body); the translation drops it, giving 'the body' rather than 'this body'.

issues.span: the most beautiful of all beings
issues.description: Latin 'illi ... qui omnium pulcherrimus est' is a personal relative ('to him who is the most beautiful of all'). Rendering it as 'the most beautiful of all beings' adds 'beings' and flattens the personal 'him who is' into a collective noun phrase; sense is largely preserved.
Latin 'occlusi sunt' (from occludo, to close/shut up) means the bodily senses are SHUT OFF / closed; 'heightened' reverses the meaning to the opposite.
'cum quo' means 'with whom/which' (referring to an antecedent); rendering it as 'this being' adds an interpretive noun not present in the Latin.

issues.span: all our bodily senses are heightened,
issues.description: Sentence ends with a trailing comma and lacks a clause boundary after 'this being', leaving the sentence run-on/incomplete.

The Latin 'cum quo' is simply a relative pronoun ('with which/whom') referring to an antecedent outside this clause. Rendering it as 'this being' supplies an interpretive noun ('being') not present in the Latin; a neutral 'with which/whom' would be closer.
Latin 'animus' and 'corporei sensus' carry no possessive; 'our' is supplied. Defensible as idiomatic generalization but strictly an addition to the source.

The Latin 'impedimento est' (double dative: 'is a hindrance/impediment to this love') asserts that lustful love OBSTRUCTS the higher love. 'An aid' reverses the sense to the exact opposite, inverting Ussher's central claim that fleshly love impedes the ascent from visible to invisible beauty.

'lubricus' here pairs with 'libidinosus' and primarily connotes 'slippery/lewd/lascivious'; 'deceitful' is a secondary figurative sense that weakens the moral-sensual force. Defensible but not the closest reading.

Latin 'lubricus' (paired with 'libidinosus') means literally 'slippery', and in this moral sense 'wanton/unsteady/perilous'; 'deceitful' is within the figurative range but shifts the emphasis from the slippery/wanton sense the collocation carries. Minor only.

The Latin 'nec ultra consurgimus' is negated ('nor do we rise further' / 'we rise no higher'); the translation drops the negation 'nec' and asserts the opposite ('we rise beyond it'), reversing the clause's meaning.
'manifestus furor est' = 'is manifest/evident madness'; 'a kind of' has no basis in the Latin and softens the categorical 'furor'.
The Latin 'furor' is simply 'madness'; 'a kind of' is an added hedge not present in the source and slightly softens the categorical 'manifestus furor est' ('is manifest madness').

The Latin 'qui diuinitus infunditur' means 'which is infused/poured in from on high (divinely)'. The English reverses the sense: 'diuinitus' = 'divinely, from God' and 'infunditur' = 'is poured in/infused', denoting divine inspiration — the opposite of human effort. 'acquired by study' contradicts the defining point of the 'good furor' (Platonic divine madness) as divinely bestowed, not learned.
The Latin sentence ends with a full stop (infunditur.), but the English omits terminal punctuation.
Latin 'in hac regione' uses the proximal demonstrative 'hac' = 'this region'; rendering it 'that region' shifts the deixis. Minor, meaning preserved.

issues.span: by dedicating it to His Mother
issues.description: Latin 'in honore suæ matris dedicando' = 'by dedicating it in honour of His Mother'; the 'in honore' ('in honour of') nuance is flattened to a simple 'to His Mother'. Sense is close but the explicit honorific framing is dropped.

issues.span: claiming that a certain revelation had been made to him
issues.description: The Latin 'cujusdam revelationis sibi factæ prætextu' uses 'prætextu' ('on the pretext of'), which carries Ussher's skeptical connotation that the revelation was a pretense/excuse. 'claiming' conveys only assertion and loses that pejorative nuance; meaning is otherwise preserved.

The Latin 'valetis' is a second-person plural verb ('you are well') but contains no explicit quantifier such as 'omnes'. English 'you are all well' adds 'all' to mark the plurality; this is a defensible disambiguation of the ambiguous English 'you', but it introduces a word not literally present in the Latin.
